titulo: Red Coloring Linked to Cancer Risk Banned in US Foods

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Text shortened by paragraphs; sentences unchanged.

parrafos: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has banned a chemical widely used to color some food products red. The ban of the coloring chemical, called dye, came nearly 35 years after it was removed from skin products because of a possible cancer risk.

The earlier ban was ordered in 1990, after two studies showed Red No. 3 caused cancer in male rats eating high levels of the chemical. At the time, however, the FDA only acted to ban the coloring mixture in products put on the skin or in drugs taken by mouth.
Health activists had long sought FDA approval to expand the ban to food products. In November, nearly two dozen members of Congress sent a letter demanding that FDA officials ban Red No. 3.
Some of the most common products containing Red No. 3 include sweets, icing, strawberry milk, maraschino cherries, strawberry protein drinks, as well as some gummy vitamins and medications.

Other countries still permit certain uses of the dye. But any imported products will still have to meet the new U.S. requirement. Red No. 3 is already banned for food use in Europe, Australia and New Zealand, except in certain kinds of cherries.

The dye will be banned in California starting in January 2027. And lawmakers in Tennessee, Arkansas and Indiana have also proposed limits on certain dyes, especially from foods offered in public schools.

Jim Jones is the FDA's deputy commissioner for human foods. He noted that even though the agency had established the new ban, “the way that FD&C Red No. 3 causes cancer in male rats does not occur in humans." FDA officials said the ban was enacted because of a U.S. rule called the Delaney Clause. This legal policy requires the FDA to ban any additive found to cause cancer in people or animals.

Dr. Peter Lurie is director of the consumer activist group the Center for Science in the Public Interest. He helped lead the latest effort to remove Red No. 3 from food products. Lurie told The Associated Press, "This is a welcome, but long overdue, action from the FDA.”

The International Association of Color Manufacturers has repeatedly said Red No. 3 is safe in levels usually taken in by humans. The group pointed to research carried out by scientific experts from the United Nations and the World Health Organization. One study, released in 2018, confirmed the safety of Red 3 in food.

Some food manufacturers have already changed their products to remove Red No. 3. One example is Sensient Food Colors, a St. Louis-based supplier of food colors and flavorings. In its place, the company uses beet juice, a dye made from insects and other coloring mixtures.
titulo_es: US bans a red food colouring linked to cancer risk
resumen_es: The FDA bans the colouring Red No. 3 in food, 35 years after banning it in cosmetics, because of a rule that requires any additive that causes cancer in animals to be removed, even though the industry considers it safe.
nivel_motivo: Product names and regulatory terms raise the measured vocabulary level, but the structure is simple and journalistic: B2.

ideas_clave.idea: The FDA has prohibited a red food dye, decades after banning it from skin products and oral drugs because it caused cancer in male rats.
The decision follows long pressure from health campaigners and members of Congress.
The dye is found in many sweets, drinks and some vitamins and medicines.
Imported goods must comply with the new rule; the dye is already restricted in Europe and elsewhere, and several US states are moving to limit dyes.
The FDA admits the cancer mechanism seen in rats does not affect humans, but a law obliges it to ban any additive that causes cancer in animals or people.
Consumer advocates welcomed the overdue ban, whereas colour manufacturers maintain the dye is safe at normal levels, citing international research.
Some companies have already switched to alternatives such as beet juice and insect-based dyes.

resumen_modelo: The text reports that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has banned Red No. 3, a dye widely used to colour foods red. The agency had already prohibited it in cosmetics and oral medicines in 1990, after studies showed that high doses caused cancer in male rats, but campaigners and members of Congress had long demanded that the ban be extended to food. The dye is present in products such as sweets, icing, strawberry milk and some gummy vitamins. Imported goods will also have to comply with the new rule, and the substance is already largely forbidden in Europe, Australia and New Zealand, while California and other states are introducing their own restrictions. Paradoxically, the FDA acknowledges that the mechanism causing cancer in rats does not occur in humans; however, a legal provision, the Delaney Clause, requires it to ban any additive shown to cause cancer in people or animals. Whereas consumer advocates welcomed this long-awaited decision, colour manufacturers insist that the dye is safe at usual levels, citing UN and WHO research. Meanwhile, some suppliers have already replaced it with alternatives such as beet juice.
